Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming
Startup Work
Hongjin Kim
Korea Advanced Institute of Science
& Technology
Republic of Korea

Igjae Kim
Korea Advanced Institute of Science
& Technology
Republic of Korea

Kwanghoon Choi
Korea Advanced Institute of Science
& Technology
Republic of Korea

Minho Ha
SK hynix
Republic of Korea

Jaehyuk Huh∗
jhhuh@kaist.ac.kr
Korea Advanced Institute of Science
& Technology
Republic of Korea

ABSTRACT
When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on de-
mand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5–11% of it is
spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation,
memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs
again even though the outcome is identical across servers or inde-
pendent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to
start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL
memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers
read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead
of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces
each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM
v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an
emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1–5.2× on
servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median
TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

1 INTRODUCTION
Serverless inference has become a common way to serve large
language models: the platform starts a worker for a model only
when the model has requests and stops it when the requests stop, so
that many models share the same GPUs [6, 7, 28]. The drawback is
the cold start. A request for a model with no running worker waits
until one is started, and this wait is part of its time to first token
(TTFT). For LLMs this wait is long, 57 to 85 s for models from 1B
to 14B with ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20 (sllm+vLLM), and hard
to avoid, because a platform cannot keep a worker ready for every
model (§3).
Most prior work reduces the cold start by loading the model
weights onto the GPU faster. Some systems make the transfer of
weights to each server faster [15, 28], and others prepare workers
and weights in advance for models they predict will be needed
[7, 16] (§2.3).
However, a cold start spends most of its time on work other than
loading the weights, which takes only 5–11%. Every new worker
compiles the model, profiles GPU memory to size the KV cache,
creates processes and imports a large serving stack, even though
another server, or an earlier start, has already done the same work.
Much of this work gives the same result on every server, or does

∗Corresponding author.

not depend on the model at all. Yet every server repeats it on every
start, and a burst that starts one model on 𝑁 servers repeats it 𝑁
times. Prior approaches either keep reusable state on individual
servers or prepare it for specific models in advance, so they do not
reuse model-specific startup artifacts across the cluster.
We classify cold-start work by two questions: does a step depend
on the model, and is its result the same on every server? The an-
swers give three classes, and Table 3 lists the techniques for the
first two. Shareable work encompasses model-specific operations
whose results can be reused across compatible servers, including
model loading, compilation, model inspection, and CUDA-graph
memory estimation. Prewarmable work does not depend on the
model: creating processes, importing the serving stack and initial-
izing CUDA. Process-bound state, the CUDA graphs, belongs to the
process that captures it. Shareable work needs to be done only once,
and prewarmable work can be done before the model is known.
Cluster-wide shared memory makes sharing this work practical.
A CXL memory pool lets every server of a cluster address the same
memory in place, and their GPUs copy from it by DMA as from
local host memory. One copy of a model’s state in the pool can then
serve every server, without a transfer per server.
We build Cairn on these ideas. The first server to start a model
publishes its weights, metadata, compile cache, compiler keys and
CUDA-graph memory estimate to the pool as immutable entries,
through a small coordinator, and every other server reads them in
place, with no checkpoint of its own. Each server also keeps a warm
container, a front-end and an engine core that have finished every
model-independent stage of startup and serve whichever model is
deployed next. Because faster cold starts leave less time to replace
a container that has been used, Cairn forks replacements from a
template process, a zygote, instead of starting them from scratch.
On two servers sharing an emulated CXL pool, with sllm+vLLM
(§5), Cairn cuts cold starts from 57–85 s to 11.0–21.0 s, 4.1–5.2×
faster. Each of these cold starts runs on a server that has never
served the model and holds no checkpoint of its own, reading only
the entries that another server published. On a one-hour request
stream that follows the Azure Functions trace, median TTFT falls
by 64%, from 32.5 to 11.8 s. In a simulated cluster of 16 servers,
timeouts fall from 15.6% to 2.1% at 3.2 requests per second. We will
release the source code of Cairn upon publication.
To summarize, we make the following contributions:
1

arXiv:2611.16180v1 [cs.DC] 12 Nov 2026

Kim et al.

• We analyze the cold start of a current LLM engine and clas-
sify its work as shareable, prewarmable or process-bound.
• We design a CXL-emulated pool that lets every server reuse
shareable artifacts that one server published.
• We design model-agnostic warm containers, replenished
from a zygote, that do prewarmable setup before the model
is known and can be applied regardless of the serving en-
gine.
• We show that Cairn makes cold starts 4.1–5.2× faster on
servers that hold no checkpoint, and lowers TTFT and
timeouts under load.

2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
2.1 Serverless LLM Inference and Cold Starts
Serverless computing is a cloud model in which users deploy their
code as functions and leave the provisioning and management of
the servers that run it to the platform [1, 20]. The platform starts an
instance of a function only when a request arrives, adds instances
as the load grows, and removes them when the load falls, down to
none when the function is idle. Users pay only while their instances
run, and the platform shares its servers among the functions that
currently have requests.
Beyond the flagship models of a few large providers, a growing
number of LLMs are deployed by users themselves. They include
open-source models used as they are, fine-tuned variants, and mod-
els trained for a particular domain or customer. Cloud platforms
such as Amazon Bedrock [2], Hugging Face Inference Endpoints
[8] and Predibase [21] now serve such models serverlessly. Users
pay only while their model serves requests, and the platform can
multiplex many models on the same GPUs.
Serverless inference is especially suited to models whose de-
mand is low or hard to predict. Most models on such platforms are
requested rarely, or in bursts separated by long idle periods [6],
as with a newly launched application or one used only at certain
times. Keeping each of them loaded on its own GPUs would leave
the most expensive and limited resource in the datacenter idle most
of the time, and its cost would fall on users whether or not they
send requests. A serverless LLM platform instead starts a worker, an
inference engine bound to one or more GPUs, only when a model
has requests, and stops it when the requests stop. The same GPUs
then serve many models over time, users pay only for the inference
they use, and a burst of requests for one model is met by starting
more workers for it [6, 7, 28].
The drawback of this approach is the cold start. A request for
a model with no running worker waits until one is started and
initialized, and its time to first token (TTFT) includes this wait.
For ordinary functions, platforms reduce cold starts by keeping
an instance alive for a while after its last request (keep-alive) and
by preparing instances in advance. These techniques bring the
cold start down to milliseconds or about a second [4, 5, 20]. Both
techniques are less effective for LLMs. Starting a worker loads giga-
bytes of weights onto a GPU and initializes an engine that compiles
the model and profiles GPU memory, which takes tens of seconds
rather than milliseconds. Keeping workers alive or prepared for

many models, in turn, would occupy the GPUs that serverless in-
ference is meant to share among models. For LLMs, cold starts are
therefore both longer and harder to avoid.
vLLM [11] is a widely used and rapidly developing open-source
LLM inference engine. A vLLM worker runs as two processes: a
front-end, which receives and tokenizes requests, and an engine
core, which owns the GPU and runs the model. In a cold start, a
newly created vLLM worker goes through six stages. In process start,
the front-end process is created and imports the Python libraries
vLLM is built on, PyTorch, Transformers and vLLM itself; these
libraries are large, and importing them takes seconds. In engine
init, the front-end launches the engine core as a separate process.
The engine core imports the same libraries again, initializes CUDA,
and sets up the executors that run the model. It also inspects the
model, reading its configuration to find which architecture to build.
In model load, the engine core builds the model’s layers in GPU
memory and copies the weights into them. The weights come from
the model’s checkpoint, the files that store its weight tensors along
with the configuration and tokenizer files needed to serve the model
[9]. They are read from storage into host memory, through the page
cache or pinned memory, and then copied to the GPU over PCIe.
The remaining stages prepare the model to run fast. In torch.compile,
vLLM compiles the model with PyTorch’s compiler [3]. The com-
piler first turns the model’s Python code into a graph. It then gener-
ates GPU kernels from this graph, merging several operations into
one kernel where it can. The compiled result is saved on disk in a
compile cache. The cache is looked up by a key computed from the
installed software, so a later start on the same server can load the
result instead of compiling again. In KV profile, vLLM decides how
much GPU memory to give the KV cache. The KV cache holds the
attention state of the requests being served. To size it, vLLM runs
the model once on dummy input at the largest batch size, which
shows how much memory a forward pass needs. It also captures
a few CUDA graphs as a trial, to estimate how much memory the
graphs will need. After setting aside memory for the weights, the
forward pass and the CUDA graphs, vLLM gives all the remaining
GPU memory to the KV cache. The last stage, CUDA graph, records
the GPU kernel launches of one decoding step so that they can
later be replayed with little CPU time. vLLM records one CUDA
graph for each of several batch sizes. However, a graph can only be
replayed by the process that recorded it. The worker serves its first
request only after this stage.

2.2 CXL Memory Pools
Compute Express Link (CXL) lets a processor access memory at-
tached to a device with ordinary loads and stores. Unlike disaggre-
gation over a network, which copies remote bytes into a local buffer,
CXL memory is part of the physical address space and is read in
place, with latency within a small factor of local DRAM [25]. A
CXL switch lets the servers of a cluster draw from a common pool
of memory devices, which reduces memory stranded in individual
servers [12, 17], and lets several of them map the same region.
Two properties of a CXL memory pool make it suited to model
state. First, every attached server can read the same copy of the data
directly, without sending it over the network. Second, to a GPU it is
host memory: once mapped and registered, the GPU copies from it
2

Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work

by DMA as from local pinned memory, with no intermediate copy.
The difficulty is coherence: when several servers write the same
region, their caches may disagree unless the hardware or a software
protocol keeps them consistent. Model state is written once and
only read afterwards, so it largely avoids this problem.

2.3 Prior Work on LLM Cold Starts
Fast weight loading. Most prior work on LLM cold starts reduces
the time to load the weights onto the GPU. ServerlessLLM keeps
checkpoints in a multi-tier store on each server and loads them
with a pipelined loader [6]. HydraServe and FaaScale distribute
a model across servers and overlap fetching with initialization
[15, 28]. However, each server still receives and holds its own copy
of the weights. Moreover, loading the weights accounts for only
5–11% of a cold start (§3.1).
Prewarming workers. Prewarming systems prepare workers
before requests arrive, so that a cold start skips part of its setup.
DeepServe keeps model-agnostic pre-warmed workers, preloads
predicted models into host memory, and sizes the KV cache offline
[7]. WarmServe keeps a pool of worker processes with the serv-
ing libraries loaded, and loads the weights of models it predicts
will be needed onto idle GPUs [16]. However, their model-specific
preparation depends on predicting the next model and stays on
particular GPUs or servers, and neither addresses how quickly a
used worker is replaced. WarmServe is also built on vLLM 0.6.3,
which by default does not use torch.compile, so its design does
not address the longest stage of a cold start in the current vLLM
(§3.1). It also runs the engine inside its API-server process and the
GPU workers as Ray actors, so the processes it prepares in advance
do not include the engine-core process that the current vLLM starts
for each instance, which repeats the imports (§3.3).
Reusing startup artifacts. Another approach saves the results
of startup work and reuses them at later starts. vLLM saves its
compile cache on local disk, so a later start on the same server
can skip compilation. Medusa materializes CUDA graphs offline
so that capture need not be repeated at startup [29]. However,
these artifacts stay on the server that produced them, and model
information, compiler keys and the CUDA-graph memory estimate
are recomputed at every start. In a related analysis, Kabakibo et al.
decompose the startup of vLLM on a single server and find that it
is CPU-bound [10].
CXL memory pools. Beluga stores the KV cache in a CXL
memory pool that GPUs on several servers access directly through
a CXL switch [27]. These servers write to the pool concurrently,
and the pool holds serving state rather than the state that a cold
start produces. Table 1 summarizes what each approach targets in
a cold start and whether its state is shared.

3 MOTIVATION
3.1 Cold-Start Latency Breakdown
Cold starts in serverless LLM inference are long, and they are hard to
avoid (§2.1). Platforms cannot keep a worker warm for every model.
Caching checkpoints in each server’s DRAM does not solve this
problem either. On a production trace, 20–46% of ServerlessLLM’s
loads miss its host cache, most often when one model is scaled

across several servers [30]. Cold starts therefore remain common
and arrive in bursts, and the length of each one matters.
Most of a cold start is not spent loading weights, so making the
transfer faster, the focus of most prior work (§2.3), leaves most of
the cold start in place. We measure the cold start of sllm+vLLM
on a server that has the serving stack installed but has not served
the model before. The server has no copy of the checkpoint in host
memory and no compile cache, and the checkpoint is on a local
NVMe disk (§6.2). It takes 57 s for OPT-1.3B to 85 s for Qwen2.5-
14B (Figure 1). Loading the weights is a small part: 6.9 s of 74.3 s
for Qwen2.5-7B, against 24.4 s for compilation, 17.2 s for engine
initialization, 12.6 s for KV-cache profiling and 7.5 s for process
start. On our system, about 90% or more of the cold start is spent
outside weight loading.

3.2 Repeated Model-Specific Work
Every server that starts a model repeats work whose result is the
same on every server. Most of a cold start produces artifacts that
depend on the model but not on the server: compiled code, model
information, Triton kernels [26], compiler keys and the CUDA-
graph memory estimate, besides the checkpoint itself. A server
that has started a model before keeps some of them on its disk
and in its memory, but a server starting it for the first time, the
common case in serverless inference, produces them all again. We
let two servers produce these artifacts independently, from empty

caches, for the 3B, 7B and 14B models. Model information, compiler
keys and the CUDA-graph memory estimate came out identical.
The estimate even matched to the byte across five runs on each
server. Compiled code and Triton kernels consist of the same files
under the same paths, and differ only in a few bytes that record
timing measurements. These artifacts are only megabytes in size,
compared with gigabytes of weights, but producing them takes
most of a cold start (Table 2).
The reads are repeated too: each server holds its own checkpoint
copy in pinned memory, and Triton’s compiled library (396 MiB)
is read in full on every cold start only to compute a cache key. A
burst that starts one model on 𝑁 servers therefore reads, loads and
compiles it 𝑁 times. The reusable state also stays only on the server
that made it, which limits the scheduler’s choices. A worker starts
quickly only on a server that already holds the model’s reusable
state, and the workers already running on that server may have to
be moved to another server to make room.

3.3 Repeated Model-Agnostic Setup
Besides model-specific work, every cold start pays for setup that
does not depend on the model, such as creating processes, importing
the serving stack, starting executors and initializing CUDA. None
of it needs to know which model will be served, yet a worker cannot
do it until a request names the model, so it lies on the critical path
of every cold start. Figure 2 shows it for the smallest and the largest
model. Apart from about 9 s of model inspection, process start and
engine initialization are this kind of setup. They take 14.4 s for

4 DESIGN
4.1 Overview
Cairn removes repeated work in two ways, summarized in §4.4
and Table 3. Work that is the same on every server is done once
and shared through a cluster-wide pool (§4.2). Setup that does not
depend on the model is done before the model is known, in a warm
container on each server. Because each cold start consumes one
warm container, replacements are forked from a template process
rather than built from scratch (§4.3). What remains is CUDA graph
capture, whose graphs are bound to the process that captures them,
so Cairn performs it as usual. Restoring captured graphs is the
subject of Medusa [29] and is orthogonal to Cairn.
Figure 4 shows the resulting flow on two servers. A deployment,
a request to start serving a model on a GPU, is handed to a waiting
warm container, which becomes the engine ( 1○). The first server to
load a model, here server A, produces its artifacts on the ordinary
path and writes them through to the pool ( 2○). Any other server,
here server B, then restores the model’s metadata, compile caches,
compiler keys and CUDA-graph memory estimate from the pool
( 3○). Its GPU copies the weights directly from the pool ( 4○). Com-
pilation, profiling and graph capture then run with most of their
work already done. Meanwhile the zygote forks the next warm
container ( 5○). Whenever a container or a pool entry is missing,
the server takes the ordinary path, so neither mechanism can make
a cold start slower than it would otherwise be.

4.2 Sharing Model-Specific Artifacts
To be reused across servers, the artifacts of §3.2 must be stored
where every server can access them. Prior systems keep them where
only one server can use them (Table 1). They store the artifacts in
a server’s DRAM or storage, transfer a copy to each destination, or
load weights into idle GPU memory by prediction. A cluster-shared
memory pool instead holds one copy that every server’s GPU reads
in place, at close to local-memory bandwidth, with capacity sized

for the cluster. Model state is also well suited to shared memory
because, unlike the KV cache [27], it is written once and only read
afterwards.
We store every shareable artifact of a cold start in the pool as
an entry. The entries of a model are its weights, stored as one
contiguous blob, its metadata, and its compile cache. The compile-
cache entry also holds the model information and the Triton kernels.
The compiler keys of the software environment and the CUDA-
graph memory estimate are stored as entries as well. Each entry is
keyed by the model and a compatibility fingerprint. The fingerprint
covers the GPU type, the versions of the engine, compiler and
libraries, and the engine options that change compiled code or
graph capture. An artifact made under a different fingerprint is
never matched, and a miss only means that the artifact is produced
on the ordinary path. Compiler keys depend only on the installed
software, so one entry serves every model.
To publish and locate these entries, a small coordinator owns the
pool’s index of entries and free space. A server that needs an entry
asks the coordinator. If the entry is valid, the coordinator returns
its location. If no server is producing it, the coordinator assigns
the entry to the server and allocates a free range for it. The server
then produces the artifact on the ordinary path and writes it to that
range, writing weights through as they are read from storage. If
another server is already producing the entry, the server waits until
it becomes valid. A burst of cold starts for one model thus produces
each entry once.
Since the pool has no hardware cache coherence across servers,
publication follows two rules. Each range has a single writer and
multiple readers (SWMR), and each entry is immutable once it
becomes valid. The coordinator marks an entry valid only after the
writer flushes the range from its CPU caches and reports completion.
Readers invalidate their cached lines of the range before reading it. If
the writer fails, the entry never becomes valid, and the coordinator
reassigns it after a timeout. Servers therefore need neither atomic
operations nor coherence on the pool.
Once an entry is valid, a server uses it according to its type. The
GPU reads the weights in place, copying them directly from the
pool with no copy in pinned memory and no local checkpoint. The
compile cache and model information are restored into the engine’s
own caches before the engine starts, so the engine finds a warm
cache and skips the work that produced it. The compiler keys and
the CUDA-graph memory estimate are instead injected into the en-
gine, which uses them rather than computing them. In addition, we
load the weights asynchronously. Compilation, profiling and graph
capture need the parameters’ addresses and shapes but not their
values, so the copy overlaps with initialization and is confirmed
complete before the first request. This also applies to weights read
from storage.
Because every server reads the same entries, a model’s state no
longer belongs to the server that produced it. A worker starts as
quickly on any server in the cluster as on the server that published
the model’s entries. Placement can therefore follow load rather than
state, and no other workers have to be moved to another server to
make room.

4.3 Prewarming Model-Agnostic Setup
Figure 5 shows the life of a warm container. A warm container is a
pair of processes, a front-end and an engine core, that has completed
all the model-independent setup of §3.3 before any model is known.
Both processes have imported the serving stack, and the engine
core has initialized CUDA and created its CUDA context. Since the
engine core is created in advance, the second round of imports in a
newly spawned engine core is avoided. The container then waits
without a model. Configuration, tokenizer, model construction,
weights, compilation, profiling and graph capture are left for the
deployment.
When a deployment request for model 𝑚 arrives, we assign the
waiting container to it ( 1○). The front-end runs the engine’s usual
startup with the deployment’s arguments, except that it uses the
waiting engine core instead of creating a new one. Specifically,
the engine core continues from configuration and model loading,
restores 𝑚’s artifacts from the pool, loads the weights, and then
compiles, profiles and captures graphs as an ordinary engine would.
As a result, the engine and the serving system above it see an ordi-
nary start. The container serves 𝑚 and exits when the deployment
ends. We do not reuse it for another model, since its engine already
holds the distributed and compilation state of 𝑚. Because a warm
container holds no model state, a single container per GPU can
serve any model without prediction.
However, each deployment consumes the container on its GPU,
and a replacement must be ready before the next deployment arrives
( 2○). Building the replacement from new processes repeats the
imports that the container is meant to save, and takes 13.9 s (§3.3).
Copying a waiting container with fork is also not feasible, because
its engine core has initialized CUDA. fork copies the memory of a
process, but not the state that the GPU driver keeps for that process.
Once CUDA is initialized, the driver maintains a CUDA context
for the process, which maps GPU memory into its address space
and relies on threads created by the driver. A child created by fork
inherits the address mappings but neither these threads nor the
context itself, and therefore cannot use CUDA. For this reason,
CUDA does not support fork after initialization, and both PyTorch
and vLLM start a new process with spawn in this case.
To address this, we fork replacements from a zygote. A zygote
is a template process that has imported the serving stack but has
never initialized CUDA, a technique also used by Android and
SOCK to start applications and serverless functions quickly [20].
Each server keeps one zygote. The engine core of a replacement is
forked from the zygote, inherits its imports, and then creates its own

CUDA context ( 5○ in Figure 4), while its front-end starts as a new
process. Since forking requires little CPU, we start a replacement
as soon as a container is taken, without slowing down the cold
start it overlaps. If the zygote cannot produce a child that initializes
CUDA, we spawn containers instead. In addition, no failure blocks
a deployment. Without a ready container, or if the handoff fails,
the deployment follows the ordinary path, and failed containers
are replaced with back-off.

4.4 Summary
Table 3 lists the techniques of Cairn by the class of work they target.
For shareable work, a shared pool holds one copy of each model’s
state for the cluster. Weights are written through to the pool on the
first load and loaded from it asynchronously. The compile cache
and model information are restored from the pool. The compiler
keys and the CUDA-graph memory estimate are injected into the
engine instead of being computed. For prewarmable work, a warm
container on each GPU has finished every model-independent step
before a deployment arrives, and the zygote replaces it as soon as
it is taken. Process-bound state, the CUDA graphs, is captured as
usual. Each technique falls back to the ordinary path when its state
is missing, so they can be enabled one at a time (§6.4).
Applicability to other engines. The cold starts of other LLM
serving engines go through stages similar to those of vLLM, so
warm containers can be applied to them as well. SGLang [32] and
TensorRT-LLM [19] also start each GPU worker as a new process,
SGLang with spawn and TensorRT-LLM through MPI even on a
single GPU. Each worker then imports the engine again, sets up
its worker objects, and initializes CUDA and its communication
library. These stages correspond to process start, the engine-core
re-import, and executor and CUDA initialization in vLLM (Figure 2).
Measured with the same stages, they take 22.3 s in SGLang and
32.5 s in TensorRT-LLM for Qwen2.5-7B, and they change by less
than 1 s across models. A warm container can therefore prepare
them in advance in either engine.
The pool applies to these engines as well. Both SGLang and
TensorRT-LLM support torch.compile as an option that is off by
default, and when it is enabled, a server can restore its compiled
code from the pool as in vLLM. SGLang also compiles some kernels
with nvcc at run time and keeps them in a cache keyed by kernel
shape. Without this cache, a cold start of Qwen2.5-7B takes 62–70 s
longer, and the cache can be reused across models whose kernels
have the same shapes.

5 IMPLEMENTATION
Cairn is implemented on a fork of ServerlessLLM [6]. Serverless-
LLM serves models with a Transformers backend by default. It also
provides a vLLM backend, but only for an earlier version of vLLM
and with limited functionality. We ported that backend to vLLM
v0.20 and its V1 engine (677 lines), including the integration of
ServerlessLLM’s checkpoint store with the new model loader. We
use the result, which we call sllm+vLLM, throughout. On top of this
port, Cairn adds 4,435 lines of code. The pool store and its tools
take 1,247 lines of Python, and the pool read path, write-through
and asynchronous load take 1,626 lines of C++ in sllm-store. The

Pool. Lacking a CXL switch, we emulate two servers sharing a
pool with two virtual machines on one host, using remote NUMA
memory as a stand-in for CXL memory as in prior work [12, 17].
A memory region on the host’s remote NUMA node is attached to
both VMs as the same shared virtual NVDIMM. Each guest maps it
as a devdax device, which exposes memory without a file system.
The guest registers it for DMA and reads it in place, as it would
a CXL pool. The coordinator’s index is a slot table at the head
of this region, updated with compare-and-swap under leases that
writers renew. The store maps an entry with mmap(MAP_POPULATE),
registers it with cudaHostRegister and issues one asynchronous
copy per tensor; write-through fills the pool and the GPU from the
same direct-I/O buffer.
Engine hooks and zygote. Compiler keys and CUDA-graph
memory estimates are injected through a vLLM plugin. The warm
container replaces the function from which vLLM V1 obtains its
engine-core process factory, so that vLLM receives the waiting child
as if it had just started it. In the zygote, libraries that query the
GPU at import time are given answers recorded in advance, and
those that need a CUDA context are imported in each child after it
creates one.

6.4 Ablation Study
To understand how much each component contributes when all the
others are enabled, we remove one component at a time from the full
system. Figure 8 shows the resulting cold start of Qwen2.5-7B. The
full system takes 16.3 s in this experiment. Every component still
matters with all the others on, and the compile cache matters most.
Without it, the cold start becomes 2.6× as long (42.5 s), because
Triton kernels are compiled again during the first profiling pass,
which also lengthens KV profiling. Removing the warm container
lengthens the cold start by 109%, removing model information by
47%, and removing the compiler keys by 9%. The CUDA-graph
memory estimate, asynchronous load and pooled weights add 0.7 s
together, shown as Others in Figure 8. The last two are small because
our baseline already holds a checkpoint copy on every server’s
NVMe: the 7B checkpoint loads from it in 3.1 s, and asynchronous
load hides that behind compilation. On this storage, the benefit is
the memory and storage a server no longer needs. With the pool, a
server keeps only 11.5 MB of metadata on its disk for the 7B model,
instead of a 15.2 GB checkpoint. We also turned on each artifact
alone, starting from a cold start without any mechanism (72.9 s).
The compile cache then saves 37%, model information 14%, and
the compiler keys and the CUDA-graph memory estimate 4% and
5%. Together, the compile cache and model information save 48%
(Table 2).

To evaluate whether warm containers are replaced fast enough to
be ready at each cold start, we run the request stream with two ways
to replace a used container, spawning new processes or forking
from the zygote. Forking prepares a replacement in 7.6 s, against

and an empty pool, and an instance is released as soon as it has no
pending request. We choose CV 1 because cold starts on a server
then often follow each other faster than a spawned replacement
can be prepared.

than 300 s, and results are averaged over three seeds.
Figure 10a varies the request rate at CV 8. Cairn achieves 2.3–
3.6× lower median TTFT than sllm+vLLM up to 3.2 requests per
second. At 3.2 requests per second, Cairn reduces the median by
3.6× and timeouts from 15.6% to 2.1%. The gap narrows only at
4.8 requests per second, where both systems saturate the GPUs
and Cairn reduces the median by only 26%. Figure 10b varies the
CV at 3.2 requests per second. Cairn outperforms sllm+vLLM by
3.6–5.2× in median TTFT at every CV and has no timeouts up to
CV 4. In Cairn, 98% of instance starts read their weights from the
pool, whereas sllm+vLLM finds them in DRAM for only 53–84%
and reads the rest from SSD.

6.7 Overheads
An idle warm container with its zygote holds 2.9 GB of host memory
(1.8 GB proportional set size, as the zygote shares pages with its
children), a 264 MiB CUDA context and 2.5% of one CPU. Pool
entries are written only once per model and configuration. Writing
through lengthens that first load from NVMe by 22–23% (3.85 s
compared with 3.12 s for 7B), because writing the pool (about 4 GB/s)
is slower than reading the disk.

7 CONCLUSION
A cold start repeats two kinds of work: work whose result is the
same on every server, and setup that does not depend on the model.
Cairn removes the first with a cluster-shared pool, from which
every server reads a model’s state instead of producing it again,
and the second with model-agnostic warm containers. Across six
models, these cut cold starts to 11.0–21.0 s, 4.1–5.2× faster, on
servers that hold no checkpoint of their own. We will release the
source code of Cairn upon publication.
